summary: Describes using HMAC with SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 in IPsec. These can provide data origin authentication and integrity checks for AH, ESP, IKE, and IKEv2, and can serve as pseudo-random functions. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: This note says how to use stronger secret-stamp methods to prove that a message came from the right sender and was not changed on the way.

subtitle: How IPsec uses HMAC with SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 to prove packets are genuine and unchanged.

tldr.problem: IPsec needs keyed hash algorithms to prove a packet came from the right sender and was not altered, and to generate keying material in IKE and IKEv2.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC combines HMAC with SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. For authentication the output is cut to exactly half its length and keys are fixed at the hash output length; for pseudo-random functions the output is not truncated and keys may vary in length.
tldr.outcome: It defines six named algorithms for AH, ESP, IKE and IKEv2, with IANA identifiers and test vectors. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 4868 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2007. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the RFC Specifies
sections.content:
RFC 4868 describes how to use HMAC together with the SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 hash algorithms inside IPsec. They serve as data origin authentication and integrity verification for the AH, ESP, IKE and IKEv2 protocols, and as pseudo-random functions (PRFs) for IKE and IKEv2.

The authentication variants are named HMAC-SHA-256-128, HMAC-SHA-384-192 and HMAC-SHA-512-256. The untruncated PRF variants are called PRF-HMAC-SHA-256, PRF-HMAC-SHA-384 and PRF-HMAC-SHA-512. Together the RFC calls them the HMAC-SHA-256+ algorithms.

Their strength depends on the secret key being unpredictable and known only to the sender and recipient.
sections.eli5: It picks three strong ways to sign network messages with a shared secret, so only people who know the secret can make or check the signature.

sections.title: Block Size, Output Length and Authenticator Length
sections.content:
The RFC defines three sizes. Block size is the amount of data the hash works on at once: 512 bits for SHA-256, 1024 bits for SHA-384 and SHA-512. Output length is the size of the hash value: 256, 384 and 512 bits respectively.

Authenticator length applies only to the authentication variants. It is the length left after truncation, and in this specification it is always half the output length.
sections.eli5: The block is how big a bite the hash takes, the output is how long the answer is, and the authenticator is the shortened answer that goes on the packet.

sections.title: Keys: Fixed for Authentication, Variable for PRFs
sections.content:
When used for authentication and integrity, a key length equal to the hash output length MUST be supported, and any other key length MUST NOT be supported. The RFC gives two reasons: shorter keys weaken security, longer keys add little, and variable lengths would create interoperability problems.

When used as a PRF in IKE or IKEv2, the key length is variable and the HMAC rules apply. A key exactly the block size is used as is. A shorter key is padded on the right with zero bits to the block size. A longer key is first hashed with the algorithm and the result is then zero-padded as needed. Shorter keys are covered because IKE or IKEv2 pre-shared keys are typically short, although HMAC strongly discourages keys shorter than the output length.

Keys MUST be generated with a strong pseudo-random function. The key distribution mechanism must give each party unique keys and give them only to the parties in the communication. The RFC also recommends periodic key refreshment, noting that weak keys such as dictionary words would resist attack far less well.
sections.eli5: For packet signing the secret must be exactly the right length. For key-making, the rules say how to stretch a short secret or squash a long one so it fits.

sections.title: Truncation and Parameter Summary
sections.content:
For authentication, the sender stores only the first half of the HMAC output (the first nnn/2 bits) in the authenticator field. The receiver computes the entire value and compares only the first nnn/2 bits. No other authenticator lengths are supported. The RFC chose half because it matches the birthday attack bound and keeps the extra bits on the wire small.

The PRF variants are identical to the matching authentication variants except that variable-length keys are allowed and no truncation is done. No extra padding is needed beyond what the SHA algorithms already define, and no implicit packet padding is required for AH. The RFC also notes no known issues with any particular cipher in ESP, IKE or IKEv2.
sections.eli5: The signature is cut in half to save space on every packet. The key-making versions keep the whole long answer.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
Section 2.7 supplies test cases with a key, data and the expected result so implementers can check their code. The PRF cases were borrowed from RFC 4231; the authenticator cases were generated with the reference code in RFC 4634. Text strings are used without a trailing null character.

The RFC warns that passing these tests only shows the algorithm is implemented correctly. It says nothing about the security of the surrounding infrastructure.
sections.eli5: These are answer-key examples. If your program gets the same answers, you probably built it right.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security rests on the strength of the hash, the HMAC construction, correct implementations, key management and key strength. At the time of writing, the RFC says there were no practical cryptographic attacks against SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512 or HMAC.

It compares these algorithms with HMAC-SHA1-96 on two axes, output length and key length. An attacker who does not know the key must guess the truncated bits, so a 128-bit truncation gives odds of 1 in 2^128 whether the hash is SHA-1 or SHA-256, and only a bias would tell them apart. Against attacks that try to guess the key, longer keys help, so these algorithms offer more security than HMAC-SHA1-96.
sections.eli5: A guesser has to get every bit of the shortened signature right. A longer secret key is also much harder to guess than a short one.

sections.title: IANA Identifiers
sections.content:
IANA assigned identifiers so peers can negotiate these algorithms. For IKE Phase 1, the hash attributes are SHA2-256 (4), SHA2-384 (5) and SHA2-512 (6). For IKE Phase 2, the authentication algorithms are HMAC-SHA2-256 (5), HMAC-SHA2-384 (6) and HMAC-SHA2-512 (7).

For IKEv2, the PRF transforms are PRF_HMAC_SHA2_256 (5), PRF_HMAC_SHA2_384 (6) and PRF_HMAC_SHA2_512 (7), and the integrity transforms are AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128 (12), AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_384_192 (13) and AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256 (14).
sections.eli5: Each recipe got a number, like a locker number, so two computers can say which one they want.
